q: Per the OEG's chapter 4 overview, which flight maneuver is added on the Commercial multi-engine test that the Private test does not require?
a: Accelerated stalls
d: Power-on stalls
Emergency descent
Steep turns
why: The Private and Commercial multi-engine task lists are nearly the same; Commercial tolerances are a little tighter, and the accelerated stall (CA.VII.D) is the added maneuver. Steep turns are on both tests, just at 50° instead of 45° for Commercial.

q: In the ACS Taxiing task, when should the brake check be performed?
a: Immediately after the airplane begins moving
d: Before engine start, with the parking brake set
At the hold-short line during the run-up
Just before turning onto the runway
why: The standard calls for checking the brakes right as the airplane starts to roll, so a problem is found while speed is low and you are still on the ramp.

q: Ground issues a taxi route different from the one you almost always get at your home field, and you start taxiing the usual way. Which ACS taxi risk is this?
a: Expectation bias about taxi instructions
d: Division of attention during preflight checks
Wake turbulence from departing traffic
Disembarking passengers on the ramp
why: Hearing what you expect rather than what was said is expectation bias, a listed taxi risk alongside route or runway changes and runway incursions. Reading back and following the airport diagram mitigate it.

q: Per the ACS Before Takeoff Check, what should you consider when positioning the airplane for the run-up?
a: The wind and any nearby aircraft or buildings
d: The departure runway heading and the current ATIS
The hold-short line and the taxi route
The field elevation and the current density altitude
why: The task asks you to position the airplane with the wind and anything behind or around you in mind, so prop blast and run-up don't endanger others.

q: In the run-up area you weigh runway length, surface condition, obstructions, and the airplane's characteristics. Which ACS before-takeoff risk are you addressing?
a: A powerplant failure during takeoff
d: Division of attention during the checks
Wake turbulence from departing traffic
An unexpected runway change by ATC
why: The Before Takeoff Check lists a potential powerplant failure during takeoff, to be assessed against airplane characteristics, runway/takeoff path length, surface, environment, and obstructions — the basis of your engine-failure plan.

q: On a Private multi-engine checkride, what is the ACS airspeed tolerance for the Vy climb after a normal takeoff?
a: +10/−5 knots
d: ±5 knots
±10 knots
+5/−0 knots
why: Private applicants must hold the manufacturer's recommended speed or Vy within +10/−5 knots. ±5 knots is the Commercial standard.

q: On a Commercial multi-engine checkride, what airspeed tolerance applies to the Vy climb after a normal takeoff?
a: ±5 knots
d: +10/−5 knots
±10 knots
+5/−0 knots
why: Commercial tightens the takeoff climb standard to ±5 knots of Vy (or the recommended speed); +10/−5 is the Private standard.

q: After a normal takeoff, how long does the ACS require you to hold Vy within tolerance?
a: Until reaching a safe maneuvering altitude
d: Until passing 50 feet above the runway surface
Until the landing gear is up and the flaps retracted
Until reaching 1,000 feet AGL
why: The task says to maintain Vy to a safe maneuvering altitude. The 50-foot point is where a short-field takeoff transitions from Vx to Vy.

q: The wind is calm on your checkride day. How does the ACS say your crosswind takeoff and landing knowledge will be evaluated?
a: Through oral testing
d: It is waived for that checkride
You must return on a crosswind day
By flying a simulated crosswind correction
why: The normal takeoff and landing tasks note that if no crosswind exists, the crosswind elements are evaluated orally — so be ready to explain the technique.

q: If the manufacturer publishes no approach speed, what does the ACS say to fly on a normal approach?
a: Not more than 1.3 times Vso
d: Not more than 1.2 times Vso
Not more than 1.5 times Vs1
Blue line (Vyse) plus the gust factor
why: Absent a published speed, the ACS standard is no more than 1.3 times the stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration (Vso), with the gust factor applied. Separately, the OEG's twin technique (3A-21) is to fly no slower than Vyse until short final with the landing assured.

q: The POH approach speed is 90 knots and the wind is calm. On a Private checkride, what airspeed range meets the ACS on a normal approach?
a: 85 to 100 knots
d: 85 to 95 knots
80 to 100 knots
90 to 100 knots
why: The Private standard is +10/−5 knots of the published approach speed: 90 − 5 = 85 and 90 + 10 = 100. A Commercial applicant would need 85 to 95 (±5).

q: A Private applicant's normal landing touches down 300 feet past the specified point, with no drift and aligned with centerline. How does this compare to the ACS?
a: Within tolerance; Private allows up to 400 feet beyond
d: Outside tolerance; Private allows only up to 200 feet beyond
Outside tolerance; Private allows only 100 feet
Within tolerance; there is no touchdown distance limit
why: For a normal landing the Private standard is touchdown within 400 feet beyond or on the specified point, and Commercial is 200 feet. The short-field standards are tighter: 200 feet (Private) and 100 feet (Commercial).

q: On a Commercial checkride, what is the ACS touchdown tolerance for a normal landing?
a: Within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point
d: Within 400 feet beyond or on the specified point
Within 100 feet beyond or on the specified point
Within 250 feet beyond or on the specified point
why: Commercial halves the Private normal-landing allowance: 200 feet instead of 400. The short-field Commercial standard is tighter still at 100 feet.

q: On a normal approach at 300 feet AGL you are 15 knots fast and can't get stabilized. What does the ACS expect?
a: Execute a timely go-around
d: Slip to bleed off the extra speed
Land long and use firm braking
Lower full flaps and continue
why: The task requires a timely go-around whenever the approach can't be flown within tolerance or anything else makes the approach or landing unsafe. Being 15 knots fast exceeds even the Private +10 limit.

q: How does the ACS want takeoff power set for a short-field takeoff?
a: Hold the brakes, set power, confirm it, then release
d: Release the brakes first, then advance smoothly
Set takeoff power during a rolling start
Set half power, release brakes, then add the rest
why: The task says to apply brakes while setting power for maximum performance and to confirm takeoff power before brake release, after lining up using the maximum available takeoff area.

q: On a short-field takeoff, how long must you hold the recommended obstacle-clearance speed or Vx?
a: Until clear of the obstacle, or 50 feet AGL
d: Until reaching 400 feet AGL
Until the landing gear is fully retracted
Until reaching a safe maneuvering altitude
why: Hold Vx (or the recommended obstacle speed) until clear of the obstacle, or until 50 feet AGL when the obstacle is simulated, then pitch for Vy. Vy is then held to a safe maneuvering altitude.

q: On a Commercial checkride, what airspeed tolerance applies to Vx during the short-field takeoff climb?
a: ±5 knots
d: +10/−5 knots
+5/−0 knots
±10 knots
why: Commercial requires ±5 knots of Vx or the recommended obstacle-clearance speed; the Private standard is +10/−5 knots.

q: On a Private checkride, what is the ACS touchdown tolerance for a short-field landing?
a: Within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point
d: Within 400 feet beyond or on the specified point
Within 100 feet beyond or on the specified point
Within 50 feet beyond or on the specified point
why: The Private short-field standard is 200 feet beyond or on the point (or threshold markings/numbers), with minimum float and no side drift. 400 feet is the Private normal-landing figure.

q: A Commercial applicant's short-field landing touches down 150 feet past the specified point, with no drift and minimum float. How does this compare to the ACS?
a: Outside; the Commercial limit is 100 feet beyond
d: Within; the Commercial limit is 200 feet beyond
Within; the Commercial limit is 400 feet beyond
Within, since there was no drift and minimum float
why: Commercial short-field landings must touch down within 100 feet beyond or on the point. 200 feet would satisfy only the Private short-field standard.

q: When you apply takeoff power on a go-around/rejected landing, what climb speed does the ACS have you pitch for?
a: Vx or Vy, as appropriate
d: Vyse, in all cases
Vxse until clear of obstacles
Vmc plus 5 knots
why: The go-around task is a two-engine maneuver: apply takeoff power right away and pitch for Vx or Vy as the situation needs (+10/−5 Private, ±5 Commercial), then hold Vy to a safe maneuvering altitude.

q: During a go-around, a departing airplane is climbing out below you over the runway. What does the ACS expect you to do?
a: Move to the side of the runway to avoid it
d: Stay over the centerline and climb steeply
Reduce power and hold altitude above it
Continue the approach and land behind it
why: The task includes moving to the side of the runway or landing area when needed to keep the conflicting traffic in sight and avoid it.

q: Per the OEG's exam tip, the ACS Go-Around/Rejected Landing task is not intended to be evaluated in what configuration?
a: Single-engine configuration
d: Full-flap landing configuration
Gear-down approach configuration
Normal two-engine configuration
why: The go-around task is meant for both engines operating. Single-engine go-around risk shows up instead under the engine-inoperative approach tasks.

q: Which is an ACS risk-management item for the Go-Around/Rejected Landing task?
a: Delayed recognition of the need to go around
d: Fuel management during single-engine operation
Management of compressed gas containers
Airport-specific security procedures
why: Go-around risks include delayed recognition, delayed performance at low altitude, power application, configuring the airplane, and a go-around after accepting LAHSO. The others belong to the single-engine instrument, oxygen, and parking tasks.

q: What bank angle does the ACS require for steep turns on a Private multi-engine checkride?
a: Approximately 45°
d: Approximately 50°
Approximately 30°
Approximately 60°
why: Private steep turns are coordinated 360° turns at about 45° of bank; Commercial applicants use about 50°.

q: What bank angle does the ACS require for steep turns on a Commercial multi-engine checkride?
a: Approximately 50°
d: Approximately 45°
Approximately 55°
Approximately 60°
why: Commercial steep turns call for about 50° of bank, 5° steeper than the Private 45°.

q: Per the OEG's ACS excerpt, what altitude and airspeed tolerances apply during steep turns (same for Private and Commercial)?
a: Altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots
d: Altitude ±50 feet and airspeed ±5 knots
Altitude ±100 feet and airspeed +10/−5 knots
Altitude ±200 feet and airspeed ±10 knots
why: Hold the entry altitude within ±100 feet and airspeed within ±10 knots throughout the 360° turn.

q: In ACS steep turns, what are the bank-angle and rollout-heading tolerances (same for Private and Commercial)?
a: Bank ±5°; roll out on the entry heading ±10°
d: Bank ±10°; roll out on the entry heading ±10°
Bank ±5°; roll out on the entry heading ±5°
Bank ±10°; roll out on the entry heading ±20°
why: Bank must stay within ±5° of the target, and the rollout must be within ±10° of the entry heading.

q: If the manufacturer gives no recommended steep-turn airspeed, what does the ACS specify?
a: Not more than Va
d: Anywhere in the green arc
Vyse plus 10 knots
At or above Va
why: Staying at or below Va keeps the structure protected because the wing stalls before the limit load factor is exceeded. Remember Va decreases as weight decreases.

q: Terrain below is 1,000 feet MSL. On a multi-engine checkride, what is the lowest altitude at which slow flight may be completed?
a: 4,000 feet MSL
d: 2,500 feet MSL
3,000 feet MSL
3,500 feet MSL
why: Multi-engine slow flight must be completed no lower than 3,000 feet AGL: 1,000 + 3,000 = 4,000 MSL. The 1,500 feet AGL figure (2,500 MSL here) is the single-engine-airplane standard.

q: How does the ACS define the airspeed to fly during slow flight?
a: Where more AOA or load factor, or less power, gives a stall warning
d: About 5 knots above the published power-off stall speed
1.3 times Vso, with the airplane in the landing configuration
The lowest speed at which altitude can be held with full power
why: Slow flight is flown just above the stall warning: any further increase in angle of attack or load factor, or reduction in power, would trigger the horn or buffet. Then fly straight, turns, climbs, and descents without a warning.

q: What are the ACS slow-flight tolerances on a Private checkride?
a: Altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed +10/−0 kt, bank ±10°
d: Altitude ±50 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed +5/−0 kt, bank ±5°
Altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 kt, bank ±5°
Altitude ±100 ft, heading ±20°, airspeed +10/−5 kt, bank ±10°
why: Private: ±100 feet, ±10° heading, +10/−0 knots, ±10° bank. The airspeed tolerance has no minus side because going slower means a stall warning.

q: What are the ACS slow-flight altitude, airspeed, and bank tolerances on a Commercial checkride?
a: Altitude ±50 ft, airspeed +5/−0 kt, bank ±5°
d: Altitude ±100 ft, airspeed +10/−0 kt, bank ±10°
Altitude ±50 ft, airspeed ±5 kt, bank ±10°
Altitude ±100 ft, airspeed +5/−0 kt, bank ±5°
why: Commercial tightens slow flight to ±50 feet, +5/−0 knots, and ±5° bank; heading stays ±10° at both levels.

q: During slow flight a gust briefly sounds the stall horn, and you immediately correct. How does the ACS treat this?
a: Not unsatisfactory, because you recognized and corrected it
d: Unsatisfactory, since any stall warning fails the task
Acceptable only on the Private, not the Commercial, test
Acceptable only if you then do a full stall recovery
why: The ACS note says a momentary warning caused by turbulence, promptly recognized and corrected, is not a failure. Continual deviation, no correction, or not recognizing it would be.

q: For an ACS power-off stall, how is the airplane configured before inducing the stall?
a: Approach or landing configuration, in a stabilized descent
d: Takeoff or departure configuration, in a stabilized climb
Cruise configuration, in straight-and-level flight
Takeoff configuration, with one engine at idle and windmilling
why: Power-off stalls simulate the approach and landing phase: set approach or landing configuration, establish a stabilized descent, then pitch smoothly to induce the stall.

q: On a power-off stall (Private or Commercial), when does the ACS have you recover?
a: Promptly after a full stall occurs
d: At the first indication of the stall warning
Before any buffet can be felt
Only after the nose drops below the horizon
why: Acknowledge the impending-stall cues, then recover promptly once the full stall occurs, using the POH/AFM procedure.

q: During a turning power-off stall on a Commercial checkride, what bank limits apply while inducing the stall?
a: Specified bank not over 20°, held within ±5°
d: Specified bank not over 20°, held within ±10°
Specified bank not over 30°, held within ±5°
Specified bank not over 45°, held within ±10°
why: The bank may not exceed 20°; it must be held within ±5° for Commercial or ±10° for Private. In straight flight, heading is held within ±10°.

q: How do the ACS stall tasks treat altitude lost during the recovery?
a: No set altitude-loss value; holding altitude isn't required
d: Altitude loss must be held under 100 feet in recovery
Altitude must be held constant throughout the recovery
Altitude loss must not exceed the POH's published value
why: The ACS notes for power-off and power-on stalls say evaluators should not require a set altitude loss or require holding altitude; recovery means reducing angle of attack first, and many factors affect the altitude used.

q: What is the minimum power setting the ACS specifies for power-on stalls?
a: No less than 65 percent power
d: No less than 55 percent power
No less than 75 percent power
Full takeoff power only
why: Power is set as the evaluator assigns, but no less than 65 percent, simulating a departure or takeoff stall.

q: In a high-performance twin, 65% power would need more than 30° nose-up to stall. What does the ACS note allow?
a: Reducing power below the ACS guideline
d: Pitching beyond 30° nose-up to reach the stall
Using a steep bank to stall sooner
Skipping the power-on stall task entirely
why: The note recognizes that some airplanes need less power to avoid excessively high pitch attitudes (over 30° nose-up), so power may be reduced below the 65% guideline.

q: For an ACS power-on stall, which configurations may the evaluator specify?
a: Takeoff, departure, or cruise
d: Approach or landing only
Landing, with the gear down
Cruise, with one engine at idle
why: Power-on stalls represent the takeoff/departure phase, so the airplane is set in takeoff, departure, or cruise configuration. Approach or landing configuration is used for power-off stalls.

q: On a Commercial checkride, when do you recover from a power-on stall?
a: First indication or full stall, as the evaluator specifies
d: Always at a full stall, never at the first indication
Always at the first stall horn, never at full stall
When the airspeed decays to the red-line Vmc
why: Commercial applicants recover at the first indication or after a full stall, as the evaluator specifies. Private applicants recover promptly after the full stall.

q: Which stall type is listed in the power-on stall risk management but not in the power-off stall list?
a: Elevator trim stalls
d: Secondary stalls
Cross-control stalls
Accelerated stalls
why: Both lists include secondary, accelerated, and cross-control stalls; the power-on list adds elevator trim stalls — the nose-up trim surprise when full power is added with the airplane trimmed for approach.

q: In the ACS accelerated stall (Commercial), what bank angle is used while increasing back pressure?
a: 45°, in a coordinated turn
d: 20°, in a coordinated turn
30°, in a coordinated turn
60°, in a coordinated turn
why: Establish a coordinated 45° banked turn and increase elevator back pressure smoothly and firmly until an impending stall. 20° is the bank limit for the power-on and power-off stall tasks.

q: On the Commercial accelerated stall, what airspeed limit does the ACS impose when setting power?
a: Not above Va or other POH/AFM limits
d: Not below Vno, the top of the green arc
Not below Vyse at any point in the turn
Not above Vx at the entry
why: Because the stall is induced with extra load factor, the entry must not exceed maneuvering speed (or other POH limits) so the wing stalls before structural limits are reached.

q: During the Commercial accelerated stall, when do you acknowledge the cues and recover?
a: At the first indication of a stall
d: After the full stall breaks
After the buffet becomes continuous
When the airspeed falls below Vs1
why: The accelerated stall is taken only to an impending stall: acknowledge the first indication (buffet, horn) and recover per the POH, then accelerate to Vx or Vy.

q: Your training twin has no oxygen equipment. In the ACS Supplemental Oxygen task, what can you still be asked to do?
a: Determine oxygen needed and brief passengers
d: Nothing; the entire task is skipped
Climb above 12,500 ft MSL to show symptoms
Obtain and install a portable system
why: Operating the equipment applies only if it is installed or available, but determining the oxygen quantity required and briefing passengers are both done for a scenario the evaluator gives.
src: OEG 4M · ACS PA.I.G/CA.VIII.A · AC 61-107 · 14 CFR Part 91

q: Which risk-management item is part of the ACS Supplemental Oxygen task?
a: Combustion hazards in an oxygen-rich environment
d: Fuel management during single-engine operation
Airport-specific security procedures
Wake turbulence in the run-up area
why: Oxygen risks are high-altitude flight, use of supplemental oxygen, management of compressed gas containers, and combustion hazards in an oxygen-rich environment.

q: The OEG lists the Pressurization task under the Commercial ACS (CA.VIII.B). When do its operate/respond/brief elements apply?
a: Only if the equipment is installed
d: On every multi-engine practical test
Only on Private-level practical tests
Only when flying above 12,500 feet MSL
why: Each skill element — operating the system, handling simulated malfunctions, and briefing oxygen use after a pressurization failure — is qualified with "if equipment is installed."

q: What bank angle does the ACS specify during an emergency descent, and why?
a: 30° to 45°, to keep positive load factors
d: 15° to 30°, to limit the total altitude lost
45° to 60°, to steepen the descent
Wings level, so the airspeed stays below Vne
why: Banking 30° to 45° keeps the load factor positive while the nose is low in a steep descent, instead of pushing over toward zero or negative G.

q: What airspeed and level-off tolerances apply to the ACS emergency descent (same for Private and Commercial)?
a: Airspeed +0/−10 knots; level off ±100 feet
d: Airspeed ±10 knots; level off ±50 feet
Airspeed +10/−0 knots; level off ±100 feet
Airspeed ±5 knots; level off ±200 feet
why: Airspeed may run up to 10 knots below the target but never above it (+0/−10), and you level off at the specified altitude within ±100 feet. These are the same at both certificate levels.

q: Calculated Vmc is 70 knots. A simulated engine failure on the takeoff roll should be given before about what speed?
a: 35 knots
d: 53 knots
65 knots
70 knots
why: The ACS note says to simulate the failure before 50 percent of calculated Vmc: 50% of 70 = 35 knots. Waiting until near Vmc would leave little margin for control. In the Seneca (Vmc 80 MPH CAS) that means before about 40 MPH.

q: On the takeoff roll, the evaluator simulates an engine failure. What does the ACS require you to do?
a: Close both throttles and stop straight, braking as needed
d: Feather the failed engine and continue the takeoff on one engine
Retard only the failed engine's throttle and stop
Rotate early and climb out at Vyse on one engine
why: Before Vmc there is no continuing: close the throttles smoothly and promptly, keep directional control, and use brakes as needed. Leaving one engine at power would yaw you off the runway.

q: You're climbing at Vyse through 250 feet AGL when the evaluator reaches for a throttle to simulate a failure. Per the ACS, this is:
a: Too low; not below 400 feet AGL
d: Acceptable, since you are at or above Vyse
Acceptable once the gear is retracted
Too low; not below 1,000 feet AGL
why: The evaluator must not simulate an engine failure after liftoff until at least Vsse/Vxse/Vyse and no lower than 400 feet AGL. Both conditions must be met.

q: After a simulated engine failure after liftoff with no obstructions ahead, what speed does the ACS have you establish?
a: Vyse
d: Vxse
Vmc plus 5 knots
Vy
why: With no obstacles, go to Vyse, the best single-engine rate of climb. Vxse (or Vmc + 5) is only for clearing obstructions; Vy is a two-engine speed.

q: An engine fails just after liftoff with obstructions ahead. What speed does the ACS have you hold until they are cleared?
a: Vxse or Vmc + 5 knots, whichever is greater
d: Vxse or Vmc + 5 knots, whichever is less
Vyse, until the obstructions are cleared
Vmc + 10 knots, then Vxse
why: Fly the greater of Vxse or Vmc + 5 knots to clear obstacles with a control margin, then transition to Vyse.

q: After you simulate feathering the propeller in the engine-failure-after-liftoff task, what does the evaluator do?
a: Sets zero thrust on the inoperative engine
d: Actually feathers the inoperative engine's propeller
Restores full power on that engine
Leaves it at idle with the prop windmilling
why: You only simulate the feather; the evaluator then sets zero thrust to mimic a feathered prop's drag. Leaving it at idle would add windmilling drag that a feathered prop wouldn't have.

q: What heading and airspeed tolerances apply in the ACS Engine Failure After Liftoff task (Private or Commercial)?
a: Heading ±10° and airspeed ±5 knots
d: Heading ±10° and airspeed ±10 knots
Heading ±20° and airspeed ±5 knots
Heading ±5° and airspeed +10/−5 knots
why: Right after liftoff the margins are tightest: ±10° heading and ±5 knots of the target single-engine speed, the same at both certificate levels.

q: After a simulated engine failure after liftoff, the airplane can't climb at Vyse. What does the ACS say to do?
a: Hold Vyse and return or go to the best landing area
d: Slow to Vxse to get more climb performance
Hold altitude by slowing gradually toward red-line Vmc
Attempt an engine restart before turning back to land
why: If no climb is possible at Vyse, keep Vyse (the best you'll get) and return to the departure airport or approach the most suitable landing area. Slowing down only reduces performance and control margin.

q: On a simulated engine-inoperative approach and landing, where does the ACS require you to touch down?
a: Within the first one-third of the available runway
d: Within 200 feet beyond a specified point
Within 400 feet beyond a specified point
Within the first half of the available runway length
why: Unlike the two-engine landings, the single-engine landing has no spot tolerance: touch down in the first third of the runway, with no drift and aligned with centerline.

q: On a Commercial checkride, the recommended single-engine approach speed is 95 knots. What range meets the ACS until landing is assured?
a: 90 to 100 knots
d: 90 to 105 knots
85 to 105 knots
95 to 100 knots
why: Commercial is ±5 knots of the recommended approach speed (95 ± 5). A Private applicant would be allowed +10/−5, or 90 to 105 knots.

q: In the ACS Maneuvering with One Engine Inoperative task, what do you do with the propeller of the failed engine?
a: Actually feather it, then restart per the manufacturer
d: Simulate feathering; the evaluator sets zero thrust
Leave it windmilling with the throttle at idle
Feather it and leave it shut down until landing
why: Here you really feather the prop, secure the engine, and then restart it with the manufacturer's procedure. The evaluator sets zero thrust only in the tasks where feathering is simulated, and the ACS limits where and how high an actual shutdown may be done.

q: The manufacturer recommends 4,000 feet AGL for engine-out training. Per the ACS, single-engine demonstration tasks must be completed no lower than:
a: 4,000 feet AGL
d: 3,000 feet AGL
3,500 feet AGL
1,500 feet AGL
why: The evaluator must pick an entry altitude so the tasks finish no lower than 3,000 feet AGL or the manufacturer's recommended altitude, whichever is higher — here 4,000 feet. In the Seneca, POH 6-12 says not to do the Vmc demonstration below 3,500 ft AGL, so that task must finish at or above 3,500.

q: Per the ACS safety note, where must the airplane be when you perform an actual feather or engine shutdown?
a: Where a safe landing at an established airport is possible
d: Directly over the departure runway at pattern altitude
Within gliding distance of a suitable open field
Within 10 NM of an airport with an operating tower
why: Tasks that need a real shutdown are flown only where you could still land safely at an established airport if the prop won't unfeather or the engine won't restart.

q: After an in-flight shutdown on the checkride, the propeller won't unfeather. Per the ACS note, how should you and the evaluator treat this?
a: As a real emergency, by both of you
d: As routine; continue the remaining tasks
As a chance to demonstrate Vmc
As a non-event if altitude can be held
why: If the engine can't be unfeathered or restarted in flight, the ACS says both you and the evaluator treat it as a real emergency.

q: You're at 2,500 feet AGL. Per the ACS, how should an engine failure be simulated?
a: Throttle to idle, then set zero thrust
d: Mixture to cutoff, then an actual feather
Fuel selector off, then an actual feather
Throttle to idle, prop left windmilling
why: Below 3,000 feet AGL, no actual shutdown: the failure is simulated by reducing the throttle to idle and then establishing zero thrust.

q: What tolerances apply in the ACS Maneuvering with One Engine Inoperative task (Private or Commercial)?
a: Altitude ±100 ft (or min sink), airspeed ±10 kt, headings ±10°
d: Altitude ±50 ft (or min sink), airspeed ±5 kt, headings ±5°
Altitude ±100 ft (or min sink), airspeed ±5 kt, headings ±10°
Altitude ±200 ft (or min sink), airspeed ±10 kt, headings ±20°
why: Hold altitude within ±100 feet — or the minimum sink rate if altitude can't be held — airspeed within ±10 knots, and selected headings within ±10°.

q: Which sequence matches how the ACS lists the steps in Maneuvering with One Engine Inoperative?
a: Memory items, identify/verify, feather, find cause, secure, restart
d: Feather, identify/verify, memory items, find cause, secure, restart
Identify/verify, restart, memory items, feather, secure, find cause
Memory items, feather, restart, identify/verify, find cause, secure
why: Keep control and do the memory items, identify and verify, feather the correct prop, try to find and fix the cause, secure the engine and watch the good one, then restart per the manufacturer.

q: Absent manufacturer guidance, how are the wing flaps and cowl flaps set for the ACS Vmc demonstration?
a: Flaps and cowl flaps both set for takeoff
d: Flaps up and cowl flaps closed
Flaps for landing and cowl flaps open
Flaps for approach and cowl flaps closed
why: The default setup mirrors the takeoff case: gear up, flaps, cowl flaps and trim set for takeoff, props high RPM, critical engine idle and windmilling, other engine at takeoff power.

q: In the ACS Vmc demonstration setup, how are the two engines set?
a: Critical engine idle and windmilling; other at max power
d: Critical engine feathered; other at max power
Critical engine at zero thrust; other at max power
Critical engine idle and windmilling; other at climb power
why: A windmilling prop creates the most drag, and full power on the good engine the most asymmetric thrust — the worst case that defines Vmc. Feathering or zero thrust would lower Vmc and make the demo unrepresentative.

q: Absent manufacturer guidance, how are the landing gear and propeller controls set for the ACS Vmc demonstration?
a: Gear retracted; propellers at high RPM
d: Gear extended; propellers at high RPM
Gear retracted; propellers at cruise RPM
Gear extended; propellers at low RPM
why: The ACS default is gear up and props full forward (high RPM), matching the takeoff/initial-climb configuration where loss of control is most likely.

q: Once configured, what airspeed does the ACS have you establish in a single-engine climb attitude before slowing in the Vmc demo?
a: About 10 knots above Vsse
d: About 5 knots above Vsse
About 5 knots above red-line Vmc
About 10 knots above red-line Vmc
why: Start in a single-engine climb attitude at roughly Vsse + 10 knots, then slow about 1 knot per second.

q: What bank angle does the ACS allow during the Vmc demonstration?
a: Not more than 5°, toward the operating engine
d: Not more than 5°, toward the inoperative engine
Not more than 10°, toward the operating engine
Wings level, with the ball centered
why: Up to 5° of bank into the good engine helps controllability and performance. Banking toward the dead engine would raise Vmc.

q: During the Vmc demonstration, at what rate does the ACS have you reduce airspeed?
a: About 1 knot per second
d: About 3 knots per second
About 5 knots per second
About 1 knot every 5 seconds
why: Raise the pitch slowly to lose about 1 knot per second, adding rudder as needed to hold heading, so the loss of directional control can be recognized clearly.

q: During the Vmc demonstration, what tells you to begin the recovery?
a: First loss of directional control, stall warning, or buffet
d: Airspeed decaying to 10 knots below the published Vsse
The airspeed reaching the red-line Vmc marked on the airspeed indicator
A heading change of 20° from the entry heading
why: Recover at the first of those three cues. Don't wait for the red line — at altitude, actual Vmc can be below it, so the stall can come first. The 20° figure is the heading limit for completing the recovery, not the cue to start it.

q: How does the ACS describe the Vmc demonstration recovery?
a: Reduce operating-engine power and lower the nose together
d: Add power on the idle engine while lowering the nose
Add full power on the good engine and pitch up to hold altitude
Lower the nose first, then reduce power afterward
why: Recover by simultaneously reducing power on the operating engine (less asymmetric thrust) and lowering the angle of attack to regain speed and control — without adding power on the simulated failed engine.

q: During the Vmc demonstration recovery, what heading tolerance does the ACS require (Private or Commercial)?
a: Within 20° of the entry heading
d: Within 10° of the entry heading
Within 5° of the entry heading
Within 30° of the entry heading
why: The recovery must be completed within 20° of the entry heading, then power is added smoothly and the airplane accelerated to Vsse/Vyse.

q: On a Private checkride, you recover from the Vmc demo and accelerate to a Vyse of 88 knots. What range meets the ACS?
a: 83 to 98 knots
d: 83 to 93 knots
78 to 98 knots
88 to 98 knots
why: Private allows +10/−5 knots of Vsse/Vyse during the recovery: 88 − 5 = 83, 88 + 10 = 98. Commercial is ±5 (83 to 93).

q: An applicant plans to start the Vmc demo by pitching steeply nose-up on both engines and then pulling the critical engine to idle. Per the ACS note, this is:
a: Hazardous and may cause loss of control
d: Preferred, since it saves altitude
Acceptable if bank stays under 5°
Required above 5,000 feet density altitude
why: The ACS specifically warns against this entry: chopping an engine at a high pitch attitude and low speed can produce a sudden loss of control. Reduce power first, then slow gradually.

q: In a normally aspirated twin at higher altitudes, why does the ACS stress recovering at the first sign of trouble in the Vmc demo?
a: Power loss with altitude can put Vmc below stall speed
d: Vmc rises above Vyse as density altitude increases
Rudder authority increases as altitude increases
Stall speed decreases below Vmc at high altitude
why: Less power from the good engine means less yaw, so Vmc decreases with altitude while stall speed doesn't. Where Vmc is below stall speed, a stall with asymmetric power can come first and lead to a spin.

q: You do not hold an instrument–airplane rating. Which ACS tasks are not required on your multi-engine checkride?
a: OEI flight by instruments and the OEI instrument approach
d: The Vmc demonstration and the OEI maneuvering task
Engine failure after liftoff and the OEI visual landing
The OEI visual landing and the OEI instrument approach
why: Both the one-engine-inoperative flight solely by reference to instruments and the instrument approach with an inoperative engine carry a note: not required without an instrument–airplane rating.

q: On a simulated engine failure in instrument conditions, the airplane can't hold altitude at the best single-engine speed. What does the ACS expect?
a: Assess performance and choose a safe-landing plan
d: Hold altitude even if the airspeed decays below Vyse
Continue to the destination as originally planned
Unfeather and restart the engine before deciding
why: The task requires assessing the airplane's capability, deciding on an action that ensures a safe landing, and never flying contrary to the engine-inoperative limitations (e.g., trading Vyse for altitude).

q: On the final approach segment of a simulated OEI instrument approach, how much course/glidepath deflection does the ACS allow (Private or Commercial)?
a: Within ¾-scale deflection
d: Within ½-scale deflection
Within full-scale deflection
Within ¼-scale deflection
why: Keep lateral and (if applicable) vertical guidance within ¾-scale deflection. The task's other tolerances are altitude ±100 feet (or minimum sink), airspeed ±10 knots, and heading ±10°.

q: On a simulated OEI instrument approach, what should your rate of descent accomplish per the ACS?
a: Reach MDA or DA/DH positioned to land straight-in or circling
d: Reach the FAF already level at the MDA or DA/DH
Stay at the MEA until the runway environment is in sight
Hold a fixed 1,000 fpm descent all the way to minimums
why: The descent rate must get you to the MDA or DA/DH positioned for a normal descent to the intended runway, straight-in or circling. If circling, you must follow the published criteria for your approach category.

q: Which is a skill element of the ACS After Landing, Parking, and Securing task?
a: A postflight inspection noting discrepancies and servicing
d: Recomputing the weight and balance for the next planned flight
Refueling to full tanks before leaving the airplane
Topping off engine oil to the maximum dipstick mark
why: The task: park in an appropriate area considering nearby people and property, complete the checklists, do a postflight inspection documenting discrepancies and servicing needs, and secure the airplane.

q: Your passengers want to walk across the ramp to the FBO while another twin is running up nearby. Which ACS after-landing risk applies most directly?
a: Disembarking passengers safely and monitoring them
d: Confirmation or expectation bias in taxi instructions
Wake turbulence behind departing or landing traffic
A runway incursion at the hold-short line
why: The parking task's risk list covers activities and distractions, airport-specific security procedures, and getting passengers off the airplane and across the ramp safely.

q: On a Private checkride, when does the ACS have you recover from a power-on stall?
a: Promptly after a full stall occurs
d: At the first indication of a stall, always
First indication or full stall, as the evaluator says
Once the nose has dropped through the horizon
why: The Private standard is to acknowledge the impending-stall cues and recover promptly once the full stall occurs. Letting the evaluator choose first indication or full stall is the Commercial standard.

q: On a Private checkride, the recommended single-engine approach speed is 95 knots. What range meets the ACS until landing is assured?
a: 90 to 105 knots
d: 90 to 100 knots
85 to 105 knots
95 to 105 knots
why: Private allows +10/−5 knots of the recommended engine-inoperative approach speed: 95 − 5 = 90 and 95 + 10 = 105. A Commercial applicant must hold ±5 knots, or 90 to 100.
